slot.brief: Ask which noble-gas fluoride does not exist / correct compositions of XeF2, XeF4, XeF6.

stem: Xenon forms several stable binary fluorides by direct reaction with elemental fluorine. Which of the following fluorides of xenon does not exist?

verdicts.working: Known stable xenon binary fluorides are XeF2, XeF4, XeF6 (even-electron species). XeF5 would have 43 valence electrons (odd, radical) and does not exist as a stable neutral binary fluoride; only ions like XeF5+ / XeF5- are known.

working:
The valence shell electronic configuration of ground-state xenon is $5s^2 5p^6$. All eight valence electrons are fully paired.

To form covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, electrons must be promoted from filled $5p$ (or $5s$) orbitals into vacant $5d$ orbitals. Each promoted electron generates two unpaired electrons. Consequently, xenon can only have an even number of unpaired electrons:
- Unpairing of 1 electron gives 2 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+2$, yielding $\text{XeF}_2$.
- Unpairing of 2 electrons gives 4 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+4$, yielding $\text{XeF}_4$.
- Unpairing of 3 electrons gives 6 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+6$, yielding $\text{XeF}_6$.

Therefore, xenon forms only the three stable binary fluorides $\text{XeF}_2$, $\text{XeF}_4$, and $\text{XeF}_6$. The neutral compound $\text{XeF}_5$ would require an odd oxidation state of $+5$ with an unpaired electron, and does not exist as a stable binary fluoride.

draft.distractor_notes:
Option A: $\text{XeF}_2$ is an existing, stable linear molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $2:1$ ratio at $673\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$.
Option B: $\text{XeF}_4$ is an existing, stable square planar molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $1:5$ ratio at $873\text{ K}$ and $7\text{ bar}$.
Option D: $\text{XeF}_6$ is an existing, stable distorted octahedral molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $1:20$ ratio at $573\text{ K}$ and $60\text{--}70\text{ bar}$; students often incorrectly assume it is sterically hindered and cannot exist.
